messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I keep running into this error: STOP ERROR in calc_uppass_scenario_probs_new2(): NAs found in sum_relprob_each_split_scenario.
All the calculations before seem to work fine and I get the usual output with all optimal parameter values, but right at the end, when the results should be written to an .Rdata object, I get this error. This is very unfortunate since the optimization process, which takes ca. 8h in my case on a cluster, needs to have finished for me to realize that there's a problem somewhere.

I'm also not sure what causes the error. It only appears when I try the trait-dependent extension (+m2). All base models (DEC, DIVA, BAYAREA) and +x models work fine. In another case, increasing the state space helped, but with this one I'm at a loss.
Have I made the estimation impossible because of constraints? but why would it work with the base and +x models then? Can the estimations be so different? Is there a way to know this before running the whole optimization process?

Has anyone else run into this error? Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,

Sarah

messages.subject: Time-stratified analysis of geologically complex regions
messages.subject_clean: Time-stratified analysis of geologically complex regions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

I have stumbled across a tricky problem in the Malay archipelago when trying to set up time-stratified models: some regions, e.g. the Philippines, Sulawesi, or the Moluccas, were independent islands for most of the geological past and reached their current composition only within the last 5 million years or so. To complicate matters more, some of these independent islands moved around a lot in the past - such as Halmahera, which super rapidly moved from north of New Guinea to the north of the Moluccas.

Currently, I have rather arbitrarily assigned just one of the "fragments" of my biogeographic regions that I track through time to estimate distances etc. for a time-stratified model. But that is not super satisfying because it oversimplifies things. Can you think of any way to keep track of the possibility that a species was on either the different fragments that make up these regions today, e.g. by coding species occurring on the Philippines as occupying two areas that had different pasts? Or do you think that would be a waste of time?

Cheers,
Ben
